general_theorem.name: SIGNED_SUBSUMPTION_MODEL_TRANSPORT
general_theorem.setup: Let A and B be CNFs over the same variable set V. Let pi be a signed permutation of V, extended to literals by pi(-l)=-pi(l). Assume that for every clause C in A there exists a clause D in B with D subseteq pi(C).
general_theorem.assignment_transport: For every assignment alpha on V define beta(v)=value_alpha(pi(v)).
general_theorem.conclusion: alpha models B implies beta models A. Therefore SAT(B) implies SAT(A), and SAT(A) OR SAT(B) is exactly SAT(A).
proof: Fix alpha satisfying B and a clause C of A.
By the certificate choose D in B with D subseteq pi(C).
alpha satisfies D, hence alpha satisfies pi(C).
By definition of beta, beta satisfies C iff alpha satisfies pi(C).
Thus beta satisfies every C in A.
general_theorem.verification_cost: Given pi and one subsumption witness per clause of A, verification is polynomial in the encoded CNF size.
general_theorem.discovery_firewall: Polynomial verification of a supplied signed-transport certificate does not prove that a suitable pi can be discovered in polynomial time on arbitrary sibling pairs. Universal polynomial discovery remains OPEN.

exact_effect: Every model of B transports to a model of A.
Therefore SAT(A) OR SAT(B) iff SAT(A).
The x2=true sibling may be deleted for SAT decision while preserving polynomial witness lifting: a surviving A model lifts to the parent by setting x2=false.
On this fixed critical instance the state rank drops exactly 2 -> 1 by destructive sibling deletion.

next_exact_question: Can a nontrivial polynomial-time discoverable subclass of signed/substitution model transports be proved sufficient on every maxdef-critical sibling pair, or can an exact counterexample refute that subclass?
